resources.string: How autonomic nerves tune heart rate
Autonomic relay to the heart

A qualitative example of normal human heart-rate control through two-neuron autonomic pathways. It shows one sympathetic route and one parasympathetic route to the sinoatrial node. Anatomy and timing are schematic.
Autonomic output leaves the central nervous system

Autonomic output adjusts how fast the heart beats without conscious effort. The first neurons in these two routes start in different places: the upper thoracic spinal cord for the sympathetic route and the brainstem for the parasympathetic route.
A relay beside the upper thoracic cord

A short preganglionic fiber leaves the upper thoracic spinal cord. In a ganglion of the nearby sympathetic chain, it passes its signal to a second neuron. That neuron sends a longer postganglionic fiber toward the heart.
The sympathetic route reaches the pacemaker

The second neuron carries sympathetic output to the sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart’s natural pacemaker. The node starts beats on its own. Stronger sympathetic input can make it fire more often, shortening the gap between beats.
A vagal relay near the heart

A long preganglionic fiber from the brainstem travels in the vagus nerve to a ganglion near the heart. A short postganglionic fiber from the second neuron reaches the SA node. Stronger vagal input can make the node fire less often.
Two relays adjust the same pacemaker

Both routes use two neurons. In this example, the sympathetic relay sits near the cord and the vagal relay sits near the heart. Both inputs can be active at once. Their levels can change independently, so normal heart rate reflects their combined influence.
